newsitem.title: UK: Swedish crown eyes further gains as budget nears.
newsitem.headline: Swedish crown eyes further gains as budget nears.

text.p: The Swedish crown looks set to extend recent gains against the mark, fuelled by optimism about Sweden's budget next week and the recent mark weakness against the dollar.

Although slightly lower in morning trade today, the crown has kept the bulk of its recent gains from the year's lows just over two weeks ago and the tone remains bullish as earlier pessimism towards the forthcoming budget looked overdone, said analysts.

"I think the concerns over fiscal policy are overstated, particularly by international investors," First Chicago international economist Teis Knuthsen said. "Sweden has a very strong external balance and is undershooting its three percent inflation target."

The crown was trading at 4.4825/55 per mark at 1248 GMT on Thursday after trading as low as 4.46 on Wednesday but some analysts see further crown appreciation to the 4.43 per mark level by the end of April.
American Express Bank senior technical analyst Gerry Celaya sees a period of consolidation followed by further crown appreciation.
"Trade has been volatile over the past few days but with the dollar up-move and favourable Swedish budget expectations, I think we'll see a move down to 4.43," Celaya said.

In his spring budget next Tuesday Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson is expected to announce a moderately expansive budget in a bid to mend the damage a series of benefit cuts have done to his minority Social Democratic party's popularity.

Leaks in Swedish media on Wednesday indicated the government had raised its budget surplus forecast to 12 billion crowns from 10 billion, more than enough to offset the strain from social spending measures worth 10 billion crowns announced in January.

Although some analysts said the 1998 budget measures failed to address underlying structural problems in the economy, the leaks indicated the goverment was likely to meet its budget targets and analysts saw little short-term risk of bond yields rising.

Analysts also said the underlying economic outlook still appeared strong with a budget deficit-to-GDP ratio below three percent, and inflation under control with consumer price data expected to show 0.5 percent growth in 1997 and 1.5 percent in 1998.

But UBS currency analyst Peter von Maydell believes that crown gains are more a result of a generally weaker German mark than optimism over Sweden's budget, and thinks the crown will continue to weaken to the 4.51 per mark level by the end of April.

"If you look at the trade weighted index the crown is near year lows and still depreciating," von Maydell said. "And budget optimism is a perverse reason to buy the crown because Sweden is not a candidate for EMU. It's not even in the ERM."
Although firmer against the mark, the crown's weakness on a trade-weighted basis still means Sweden has little room to cut interest rates, said Standard Chartered treasury economist Tim Fox.

"There are concerns the trade-weighted index undervalues the crown and Sweden's Riksbank wants to see it between 109 and 118," Fox said. "I think it's fair value in its present range (around 122). Mark/crown would need to be below 4.40 before the crown is under 120 on the trade-weighted index again."

It looks likely Sweden will stay out of the first wave of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) in a "wait-and-see" approach to gauge the success of the single currency's start even though analysts said it looked set to meet the Maastricht treaty's economic criteria for the first wave in 1999.
First Chicago's Knuthsen believes Sweden will choose to opt out when parliament makes its decision this autumn.
"It's very likely they'll choose to stay outside even though they don't have a formal opt-out," Knuthsen said.
Sweden's intention to join the ERM or ERM2 post January 1999 with the view to joining the single currency means the crown is likely to gain on the coattails of any EMU optimism.
However, analysts were cautious that the Swedish electorate's current distaste for joining EMU could see this relationship dissolve, with potentially negative results for the crown.
